In these records the Lord, though the creator of heaven and earth, is said to value even the prayer of the poorest man (131:7.2).
131:105: The Shinto records especially warn against pride. Pride hides God; even a single hair of pride blocks the light of salvation like a great cloud. Prayer is heard, they say, when one comes with a clean heart free of falsehood and hypocrisy, a soul that reflects truth like a clear mirror (131:7.3).
131:107: Melchizedek's messengers went as far as China, and of the many Chinese religions the most lasting, and the one containing the most monotheistic truth, was Taoism (131:8.1). The Supreme One of Taoism existed before heaven and earth came to be; he stands alone and does not change, and as the mother of the world he sets all creation in motion (131:8.2).
131:108: Taoism likens true goodness to water. Like water it blesses all things and harms nothing, and it seeks out the lowest places that others shun (131:8.3). The Supreme nourishes without forcing, leads without self-assertion, and helps progress without domineering (131:8.3).
131:110: God does not reward man for what he does but for what he is. (131:8.5)
131:113: Even the great religion of the world that recognizes God least acknowledged the monotheism of the Melchizedek missionaries and their successors (131:9.1). The Confucian records say that what Heaven appoints is without error, that benevolence is the greatest gift Heaven gives to man, and that man's virtue is the fruit of the nobility Heaven bestows (131:9.2).
131:114: These records see faith as the foundation of life. If there is virtue in me, it is a manifestation of Heaven dwelling with me; and they confess that they do not know how a man can live without good faith (131:9.3). The spirit of the noble man, they say, ascends after death to the glorious light of final brightness (131:9.4).
131:116: After the hard labor of arranging the teachings of the world's religions, Ganid set down the faith he had reached through Jesus' teachings. He used to call this faith "⟦Q 131:10.1⟧our religion⟦/Q⟧" (131:10.1). It begins with loving the one God with all one's mind and heart, and loving all his children as oneself (131:10.2).
131:117: Almost every one of the ten religious records Ganid collected contained the same one rule: treat others as you would like to be treated. The form differed a little in each, but the root was one.
131:122: The evil you would not have done you, do not to others (131:1.7)
131:124: What you hate, do not to others (131:2.11)
131:126: Do not to others what you would not wish done to you (131:3.6)
131:128: Do to no one what would be repugnant to yourself (131:4.6)

131:132: What you do not like done to yourself, do not to others (131:9.4)
131:134: Whatsoever I would that men should do to me, I will do to them (131:10.7)
131:136: Ganid's confession goes one step further. He does not stop at believing that God is the Father of all peoples; he says that from now on he will believe that God is his own Father (131:10.5). And while it sometimes frightens him to think that all men are his brothers, he realizes that he cannot rejoice in the fatherhood of God while refusing the brotherhood of man (131:10.7). He sees God in other religions too, but his conclusion is that the God of our religion is more beautiful, more lovable, and more personal (131:10.8).
131:138: ⟦Q 131:10.8⟧At last I have a religion with a God, a marvelous God, and he is a God of eternal salvation.⟦/Q⟧ (131:10.8)
131:141: Paper 131 looks like a catalog of world religions, but beneath it runs a single story. The seed of the one God sown by the Melchizedek missionaries who set out from Salem grew in different forms in Palestine and India, Persia, China, and the Far East. Gathering those traces one by one, Ganid saw that everywhere the witness lived on that God is far away yet dwells within our hearts, and that we should treat others as we would like to be treated. And at the end of his long collecting he arrives at the simplest truth he learned from Jesus: God is my Father, and therefore all men are my brothers.

132:1: In Rome, the capital of the world, how did Jesus prepare the way for the gospel by truth alone, without attacking error?
132:4: In Paper 131 Ganid gathered the records of the world's religions in Alexandria. Paper 132 shows the six months after the party reached Rome. On their third day in Rome the three met the Emperor Tiberius, and after they left the emperor pointed to Jesus and said that if he had that man's kingly bearing, he would be a real emperor (132:0.1). Jesus' chief reason for agreeing to this journey was his desire to study and mingle with the mortals gathered from every part of the world (132:0.3).
132:5: The most valuable work of the stay in Rome was his contact with religious leaders. Jesus made intimate friends of thirty-two of them: five Stoic philosophers, eleven Cynics, and sixteen leaders of the mystery cults. He never once attacked their errors; instead he picked out and brought to light the truth in what they taught, so that this truth would crowd out the error (132:0.4). Thirty of them later became pillars of Christianity in Rome, yet they never knew who the scribe of Damascus had been (132:0.5, 0.9).
132:6: What, then, did Jesus give to the philosophers and priests of this city, to its senators and slaveholders, to a lost child and a widow?
132:8: ⟦Q 132:3.2⟧Truth cannot be defined with words, only by living.⟦/Q⟧ (132:3.2)
132:12: The writers of this paper say that behind the rapid spread of Christianity throughout Europe lay three most important factors. The third was the preparation of these thirty men in Rome (132:0.5-0.8).
132:14: Three factors in the spread of Christianity
132:17: Choosing him as an apostle and holding on to him
132:19: His death led to the winning of Saul of Tarsus
132:21: Preparing them in advance as leaders of the new religion in the empire
132:23: Early in his stay in Rome Jesus talked all night with Angamon, a leader of the Stoics. He taught that the standard of true values must be sought on the level of the spiritual world and eternal reality, and that all material standards are temporary and partial (132:1.1-1.2). A scientist, as a scientist, should confine himself to discovering the relations of material facts; the moment he asserts materialism or idealism, he is already doing philosophy (132:1.2).
132:24: Unless moral insight and spiritual attainment grow along with it, the progress of a purely materialistic culture will in the end threaten civilization (132:1.3). Scientist and religionist alike stand before the bar of human need; rather than fighting each other, they should justify their existence by service to human progress (132:1.4).
132:26: Mardus, the leader of the Cynics of Rome, asked about good and evil (132:2.1). Jesus answered that good and evil are words expressing relative levels of human understanding of the universe. The lazy man takes social convention or religious tradition as his standard of good, but the soul rising toward eternity must make living personal choices by the standards set up by the indwelling spirit (132:2.2).
132:35: Becomes a slave of religious authority
132:37: Experience is good when it deepens the appreciation of beauty, strengthens the moral will, and enlarges the ability to love and serve one's fellows (132:2.5). Until we reach Paradise, goodness is more a quest than a possession (132:2.8). The possibility of evil is necessary for moral choice, but the actual experience of evil is not. Evil becomes real only when a moral mind chooses it (132:2.10).
132:39: ⟦Q 132:2.10⟧Evil becomes a reality of personal experience only when a moral mind makes evil its choice.⟦/Q⟧ (132:2.10)
132:42: Nabon, a high priest of the Mithraic cult, tried instead to convert Jesus, not knowing that he himself was being prepared as one of the early converts to the gospel of the kingdom (132:3.1). Jesus taught him that truth is always more than knowledge (132:3.2).
132:54: The religious experience of spiritual living
132:57: Because man is lazy and fears the unknown, he tries to fix science, formulate philosophy, and crystallize truth into creeds (132:3.3). But truth cannot become man's possession without faith, for a man's thoughts and ideals can never rise higher than his faith—his sublime hope (132:3.5). Just as plants and animals survive by passing on the same particles to the next generation, the soul of man survives death by becoming one with the indwelling spark of divinity (132:3.6).
132:58: Spiritual evolution is an experience of choosing the good more and more willingly, and to that extent the possibility of evil diminishes (132:3.8). To attain the perfection of spiritual self-control is to attain the perfection of freedom (132:3.10).
132:60: In Rome Jesus met people of every race and class. He had two purposes: to learn how they reacted to life, and to say or do something that would make that life richer (132:4.1). He usually opened a conversation with questions, and he talked least with those he taught most. Those who gained the greatest benefit were people weighed down by burdens and worries (132:4.2). In this way he made affectionate contact with more than five hundred people (132:4.3).
132:65: All his life advocated the policy that the people support the government
132:67: Freed one hundred and seventeen slaves the next day
132:69: Realized that his patients were beings of body, mind, and soul
132:70: A Roman soldier by the Tiber
132:71: Be brave not only in hand but also in heart
132:72: Marcus, an orator in the forum
132:73: Later preached the gospel as a successor of Peter
132:75: With Jesus' defense the case was reopened and he was released
132:77: Defending the poor man, Jesus said that justice makes a nation great. Woe to a nation where only those with money and influence can obtain ready justice; civil government is founded on justice, and true religion on mercy. This was the nearest he came to a public appearance in his personal ministry (132:4.8).
132:79: A wealthy Stoic citizen, introduced by Angamon, asked whether he should keep his wealth or give it away. Jesus made clear that his advice was for this one man only, not for other rich men, and then urged him first to examine honestly where his wealth had come from (132:5.1-5.2). He then went through ten ways of accumulating wealth and the attitude to take toward each (132:5.3-5.24).
132:84: Pass the lawful share on to the next generation; share out the unjust share
132:86: Take a reward, but provide for many fellows to share
132:88: Take only the fair profit you would allow others
132:90: Return it to those exploited, or to their descendants
132:92: First clean up the capital; take no usury
132:96: Regard it as a trust for the good of one's group
132:98: Hasten to make full restitution to the rightful owners
132:100: Do not endanger them; take only an honest share
132:102: Truly one's own, so long as it harms no fellow
132:104: Jesus said that when in doubt he should decide in favor of the needy, those who suffer undeserved misfortune; God would not condemn him for erring on that side (132:5.13). The rich man promised to begin managing his estate according to this counsel the very next day (132:5.25).
132:106: In Rome the Creator of a universe spent several hours taking a lost and crying boy back to his mother. Jesus told Ganid that most people are like this child: they are not far from safety, yet they spend their lives weeping in fear and sorrow. And he said that one who knows God should regard guiding his fellows not as a duty but as a privilege (132:6.1). From that day Ganid sought out lost children all his life.
132:107: The two visited many times the home of a widow who had lost her husband in an accident and was raising five children; they provided food and clothing and even found work for the eldest son (132:6.2). When Gonod laughed that Jesus was trying to make his son a philosopher or a philanthropist, Jesus answered that if he became all four, he could hear the melody of life fourfold. When urged to write a book, he said his mission was not to write books but to live a life for this generation and all generations (132:6.3).
132:109: On the way to the lakes of northern Italy Jesus did not speak to a certain pagan they met, because the man was not hungry for truth. God cannot be revealed to one who is not seeking him, Jesus taught; the real work of one who knows God is to live so that the Father is revealed through his life (132:7.1-7.2).
132:110: In the Swiss mountains, when Gonod asked about Buddha, Jesus answered that Buddha was a great man but an orphan prophet who early lost sight of his spiritual Father. His ship ran aground just outside the harbor of salvation because of faulty charts of navigation (132:7.4).
132:117: Did not clearly discover him in mind
132:120: Largely failed to know him in spirit
132:128: When Ganid proposed that they make a new religion together, Jesus answered that religion is not made but grows, and that the revelation of God flashes out in the lives of those who reveal God to their fellows (132:7.6). Ganid did not know it, but at that very moment they were in fact making a new and eternal religion that reveals God to man through Jesus (132:7.9).

132:133: Paper 132 shows the six months Jesus spent in the capital of the world. To philosophers he gave true values and truth; to a priest, faith; to a rich man, the way of stewardship; to a poor man, justice; to a lost child, the way home. Nowhere did he attack error; he brought to light the truth people already had and let that truth crowd out error by itself. The minds of the thirty men prepared in this way later became the field that received the gospel. And his talk with Ganid gathers the meaning of all this into one sentence: religion is not made but grows in lives that reveal God.

132:140: Evil becomes real only when a moral mind chooses it

133:1: On the way back from Rome, what did Jesus teach about mercy and justice, soul and mind, and how did he part from Ganid?
133:4: In Paper 132 Jesus spent six months in Rome, meeting religious leaders and a great many other people. Paper 133 is the return journey, from leaving Rome until he parted from Ganid and his father in Mesopotamia. Jesus left without saying good-by to anyone, and the Stoics, Cynics, and members of the mystery cults who had known him kept meeting in small groups, remembering his teaching, until the Christian preachers arrived (133:0.1).
133:5: The party walked down the Appian Way to Tarentum, meeting all kinds of people (133:0.2). When Ganid asked on the road about the caste system of India, Jesus answered that though men differ in many ways, all mortals are equal before God. In God's eyes there are only two groups: those who desire to do his will and those who do not (133:0.3).
133:6: Now, passing through Corinth and Athens, Ephesus and Cyprus, Antioch and Ur, what did Jesus teach about mercy and justice, and about science, soul, and mind?
133:8: ⟦Q 133:0.3⟧God is truly no respecter of persons.⟦/Q⟧ (133:0.3)
133:12: By the roadside near Tarentum a bully was beating a small boy. Jesus rescued the boy and held the attacker until the boy had escaped. But when the bully was released and Ganid started to thrash him, Jesus at once stopped him. Ganid protested: if mercy says to rescue the weak boy, does not justice say to punish the wrongdoer? (133:1.1).
133:18: Always the work of the individual
133:21: A function of society, government, or universe administration
133:24: Jesus explained that since no two people are likely to agree about punishment, the administration of justice is entrusted to the group, to its representatives, to those who know all the circumstances (133:1.2). Asked what he would do if someone attacked him, he said that he would defend himself without hesitation against a creature with no moral judgment, but that he would not punish a fellow man in advance without trial; he would restrain and persuade him. He was absolutely sure that the whole universe was friendly to him (133:1.4). At another time he also said that organized society has the right to use force in carrying out its just mandates (133:1.5).
133:26: At the dock a man was beating his wife. Jesus tapped him lightly on the shoulder, asked to talk with him privately, and asked what terrible thing had happened that a strong man should attack the mother of his children before everyone. What moved the man was not so much the words as the kindly face and sympathetic smile, and he repented of his lack of self-control (133:2.1).
133:27: Jesus told him that a man has no rightful authority over a woman unless she herself gives it. Man and woman are partners with God in that together they create beings with the potential of immortal souls, and he should love and cherish his wife as the Father honors the Infinite Spirit (133:2.2). Hearing this, Gonod resolved to rebuild his home when he returned to India (133:2.3).
133:29: ⟦Q 133:2.2⟧The loving care and consideration which a man is willing to bestow upon his wife and their children are the measure of that man's attainment of the higher levels of creative and spiritual self-consciousness.⟦/Q⟧ (133:2.2)
133:32: In Corinth Ganid became very interested in the Jewish religion and liked to observe the home of Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue. Meanwhile Jesus met with Crispus more than twenty times and taught him a better way of faith. Later, when Paul was driven out of this synagogue, Crispus and his whole family accepted the new religion (133:3.1-3.2). Aquila, the Cynic Jesus had met in Rome, also helped Paul together with Priscilla (133:3.12).
133:33: One evening, when two courtesans approached, Ganid sharply tried to drive them away. Jesus asked who we are to judge these women, and said they were not willfully evil but had yielded to pressure in despair (133:3.6-3.7). Ganid apologized, and Jesus took the two women to the home of Justus and asked his wife Martha to help them begin a new life. One of them died in the hope of eternal survival, and the other became a lifelong member of the first Christian church in Corinth (133:3.8-3.10).
133:35: Of the people Jesus met during two months in Corinth, more than half later became members of the Christian community (133:3.11). Jesus gave each person words fitted to his work and situation (133:4.2-4.12).

133:42: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's

133:60: Appeal for forgiveness to the One who judges by true motives
133:63: At an inn in Athens, after a Greek philosopher had lectured on science for nearly three hours, Jesus spoke. He said that the scientist may measure the forces of gravity, light, and electricity, but he cannot tell us scientifically what they are (133:5.3-5.4).
133:72: The wisdom that correlates quantitative and qualitative observations
133:74: Logic and mathematics are reliable in the material world but not in the problems of life. If one man can shear a sheep in ten minutes, ten men cannot shear it in one minute. On the other hand, a union of personalities working in harmony produces far more power than a simple sum (133:5.5-5.6). When the mind thinks of quantitative facts and qualitative values as having a common cause in the Paradise Father, it can see the unity of the universe, and the real universe is friendly to every child of God (133:5.8).
133:76: In Ephesus Ganid even bought a small silver shrine of the temple of Artemis, and that night there was a long talk about worshiping things made by human hands (133:6.1). When a progressive philosopher of the city asked what Jesus meant by the word "soul," which he so often used, Jesus explained as follows (133:6.4).
133:81: The self-reflective, truth-discerning, spirit-perceiving part of man
133:85: When mind first acts morally, the Adjuster comes and the soul is born
133:89: The self-realization of moral consciousness, spiritualized, gains survival value
133:91: Disharmony between moral and intellectual self-consciousness
133:93: A stagnant soul is a dying soul (133:6.5). Neither material science nor purely spiritual tests can prove the existence of the soul, yet every morally conscious mortal knows the existence of his soul as a real personal experience (133:6.7).
133:95: While they were resting in the mountains of Cyprus, Ganid suddenly came down with a severe fever. On that mountain, far from any dwelling, Jesus nursed him skillfully and tenderly, and Gonod marveled at his gentleness (133:7.3). After his recovery Ganid asked what it meant that man experiences a higher self-consciousness than the animals, and Jesus stressed that self-consciousness is a reality. If any animal became self-conscious, it would become a primitive man (133:7.5-7.6).
133:96: An idea is not a mere record of sensations; it is sensation plus the reflective interpretation of the self, and the self is more than the sum of its sensations (133:7.7). People differ so greatly in life not only because of heredity and environment, but also according to how far they have become one with the indwelling spirit of the Father (133:7.11).
133:98: ⟦Q 133:7.12⟧The supremely happy and efficiently unified mind is the one wholly dedicated to the doing of the will of the Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧ (133:7.12)
133:100: The human mind cannot endure a double allegiance, serving good and evil together. True peace is gained not by giving up noble longings or compromising ideals, but by overcoming evil with the power of good and firmly asserting the triumph of what is true (133:7.12).
133:102: Antioch was the third city of the empire and the first in immorality. Jesus did not go with them to the groves of Daphne, and as Palestine drew near he grew more and more serious and thoughtful. When asked why he took no interest in this city, he said only that someday he would come back here (133:8.1-8.2).
133:103: Here Ganid put Jesus' teachings into actual practice. He went to see a discontented Indian employee who was about to be dismissed, talked to him about the Father in heaven, and shared a Hebrew proverb: whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might (133:8.3).
133:105: On the caravan journey across the desert, when Jesus offered to load the camels and drive them himself, Ganid exclaimed, Is there anything you cannot do? (133:9.1). At Ur, the birthplace of Abraham, the two talked long about the difference between knowledge, wisdom, and truth (133:9.3).
133:106: At last, at Charax, the day of parting came. Ganid said that the Father in heaven must surely be something like him, and that above all he would never forget him. Gonod thanked him as the one who had made them better men and helped them to know God (133:9.4). They never learned that Jesus of Nazareth was their teacher Joshua. Ganid returned to India, became his father's successor, and spread widely the truths he had learned from Jesus (133:9.4-9.5). Thus ended the chapter that may be called the mission of Joshua the teacher (133:9.6).
133:108: Paper 133 is the story of the cities Jesus visited on his way back from Rome, but it is really the story of the people he met along the way. He stopped a fight and sorted out the parts of mercy and justice; he gave a wife-beater the true authority of a husband, courtesans the chance of a new life, and a miller, a judge, and a condemned man each a truth to hold in his own place. In Athens, Ephesus, and Cyprus he unfolded science, soul, and mind in turn, showing that facts and values alike are united in one Father. And as Ganid's parting words show, what lasted longer than all these teachings was the teacher himself, so like the Father in heaven.
